summary: Scenery: rock, timber, masonry, thatch, foliage. What Lorencia is built out of, standing in the open where the light finds it.
why: The pad is wrap, and that is the whole reason this is a profile rather than a copy of
the weapon one. A weapon sheet is an atlas - a blade in one corner, a grip in another -
so its border replicates, because wrapping would feed the grip's browns into the blade's
edge. A world sheet is the opposite thing: ston01 is a rock face that fills its whole
128 square with no seams in it, tile_ston04 and tile_wood02 say what they are in their
names, and the game lays them next to themselves. For those the texel past the right
edge really is the texel at the left edge, and telling the model otherwise makes it
resolve a border the game then butts against its own opposite side.
That key had been written in both profiles since they were made and was reaching
nothing - settings.py dropped it and upscale.py had 'edge' as a constant - so the first
thing this profile needed was for its own setting to exist.
Upscale 3x at detail 0.65, the same as the item profiles. It was tempting to argue for
less on the grounds that scenery is seen from further away, and it is wrong: a wall is
further off than a sword only until you walk up to it, and MU's camera puts the player
against buildings constantly. The distance an asset is *usually* seen at is not the
distance it has to survive.
default_material is rock. Lorencia's object list is thirteen trees, five stones, six
stone walls, four wells and a lot of masonry, so stone is what an unlooked-at island is
most likely to be - and unlike 'unassigned' it produces something that can be judged on
the first build.
tiled is the setting that matters most and it is not a number. World art repeats - a wall
sheet is laid next to itself and a boulder wraps its rock face round twice - so each
triangle samples its sheet more than once and there is no unique layout to bake it into.
Stone01 proved it: baked, the boulder was 84% of the triangles and held 18% of the map
while thirteen identical grass cards took 59%. Tiled, MU's sheets ship as MU drew them,
the mesh keeps MU's coordinates, and thirteen identical cards cost one sheet because they
genuinely are one sheet.
What it gives up is the generated surface. The grain normal and the traced occlusion are
baked into an atlas and have nowhere to live on a repeating sheet, so roughness and
metallic come through as factors and the normal map is absent. That is a real loss and it
is smaller than the one it replaces: a boulder at a third of the texel density it needs is
not improved by a grain map over the top of it. Per-sheet tiling maps, generated at the
sheet's own size rather than baked, are the way to get it back.
default_material stops meaning much here. A tiled asset assigns per sheet, through
sheet_materials, because that is the level at which the question has an answer: ston01 is
rock everywhere it appears. This remains the fallback for a sheet nobody has named.
upscale_why:
The same choice the tiles made, for the same reason and with the same measurement. A wall is a large flat surface seen at a distance, which is what a tile is; it is not a sword hilt.

Through the whole pipeline, against a plain Lanczos resize: c_wall04 goes from 1.13x to 2.47x, tile_ston06 from 1.18 to 2.42, the cart sheet from 1.09 to 2.08, the bookshelf from 1.14 to 1.82, the tombstone from 1.11 to 1.99, the well from 1.08 to 1.70. The photographic model was giving these about a tenth over doing nothing.

Items keep it. The drawn model at full strength turns the ribs on Kris's guard into hard rectangles with dark outlines — the chain that upscale.py has warned about since it was written — and armour and weapons are looked at from a hand's distance where that is the whole of what you see.
play_speed_why:
CreateObject's `o->Velocity = 0.16f`, which is the play speed every world object gets before any world's switch touches it. MoveObject hands Velocity to PlayAnimation exactly where a character's play speed goes, so it is the same field under another name.

Here rather than on each asset because it is the default and not a decision. Without it every animated object in the project took export_gltf's own default, which is the townsperson's 0.25 out of OpenNpc - so Lorencia's trees, its lamps, its curtains and all 22 of Noria's animated models ran at 6.25 keys a second against MU's 4.0. 56% fast, on everything, and invisible unless you had the client open beside it: a swaying tree that is half again too quick still looks like a swaying tree.

An asset overrides where MU's own per-world switch does. Lorencia's, from CreateObject: MODEL_TREE01 and +1 take `1.f / o->Scale * 0.4f` - a speed that depends on the placement's scale, so a big tree sways slower - the street light, the candle and the two signs take 0.3, and the treasure chest takes 0.f, which is `still` rather than a speed. Noria's arm sets no velocity at all, so every one of its objects is this.
